en: Record of the Transmission of the Buddha’s Mind-Seal of Tiantai,
composed by the monk Huaize of Huxi, the Great Master Who Propagated the Teachings of the Tiantai School and Sect.
The single character "only" (zhi) further clarifies that our present school maintains that goodness is inherently complete within the nature;
other masters also recognize that evil is complete within the conditions and the understanding.
None could fathom this;
thus we know that the merit of the Tiantai school lies in the inherent nature,
and that this merit resides in the inherent evil (xing-è).
If it were necessary to destroy the nine realms of innate evil in order to manifest the Buddha-realm of innate goodness,
this would constitute the severance of the nine realms based on principle; however,
this is not what is being discussed here.
Therefore, the ten vehicles of wondrous contemplation elucidated in the *Zhi Guan* (Stopping and Contemplation) take the ten objects—
such as the five aggregates— as well as the three obstacles and four demons,
and contemplate each of them so that they all become the perfect and wondrous Three Truths.
This is the fundamental framework for generating the resolve and establishing practice.
How could there be a more perfect or sudden method than this?
One who begins their practice must first focus on the internal mind when cultivating contemplation.
Therefore, among the three categories [of aggregates, bases, and elements], one sets aside the bases and elements;
furthermore, among the five aggregates, one excludes the first four and specifically takes the aggregate of consciousness as the object of contemplation.
It is like setting aside the *zhang* to focus on the *chi*, or setting aside the *chi* to focus on the *cun*;
this constitutes the mind of total ignorance (*avidyā*).
If one proceeds from the general to the specific, it is the sixth consciousness (*ṣaṣṭhavijñāna*).
It is like cutting down a tree by reaching its roots,
or cauterizing a disease by finding its vital point;
thus, a thousand branches and a hundred ailments will naturally wither away.
If one does not enter [the path] therein, one subsequently proceeds through the remaining examples of the single mind and the other aggregates (skandha) and bases (āyatana).
This continues until the nine objects, which are observed only when they arise;
those that do not arise are not observed, yet this applies to all without exception.
This clearly reveals that the cultivated evil of the three paths within the nine realms is,
in its very essence, the dharma-gate of inherent evil (xing-è).
Because inherent evil is all-pervasive and interfused, there is no phenomenon that does not partake in it.
Spontaneously encompassing the goodness of the Buddha-realm nature,
since cultivated evil is itself the evil of the nature, there is no cultivated evil to be refuted and no evil of the nature to be revealed.
This constitutes total evil;
it is only through this evil that the meaning is fully established.
This is precisely how our school clarifies that [the nature of evil] is eternally distinct from that of other masters.
Since it is neither the union of two distinct entities nor the turning over of one side to the other,
it must be that the very substance itself is entirely so for it to be called "identity. Why,
then, would it be necessary to sever afflictions and birth-and-death?
Only then can the Buddha-realm, bodhi, and nirvana be clearly manifested.
Furthermore, one must understand that this nature— whether good or evil—
is designated by different names across the various Mahayana teachings.
Regarding the differences between the extensive and the concise,
and the variations in their designations,
the *Avataṃsaka* states:
Capable of following conditions of defilement or purity,
they consequently differentiate into the ten dharma-realms;
when deluded, all ten realms are defiled.
Upon awakening, the ten realms are all pure.
When the three characters for the ten dharma-realms are read as separate syllables, the three causes are fully present;
when the three characters are pronounced together, they signify the nine realms.
Evil has the realm of phenomena as its direct cause;
the Buddha-realm has the realm of phenomena as its direct cause.
The ten characters alone invoke the Dharma-realm.
When the ten dharmas are pronounced together, they constitute the "causal factor of realization" (了因); when the character for "realm" (界) is pronounced alone,
it constitutes the "causal factor of conditions" (緣因).
The Lotus Sūtra states:
"The true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena does not transcend the provisional and the real.
All phenomena are the good and evil conditions and causes within the provisional that is of the same essence (*tongti*).
The true aspect (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) is the single essence within reality that serves as the direct cause for both good and evil.
The ten suchnesses of the nine realms constitute the indirect cause for evil,
while the ten suchnesses of the Buddha-realm constitute the indirect cause for good.
Having read it three times, one understands that it is complete and without deficiency.
In the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*,
it is taught that both the icchantika and the virtuous person possess both the nature for goodness and the nature for evil.
This is called the causal condition of good and evil.

Since these three causes are wondrous, when words are present as conditions, they must necessarily possess understanding; when understanding is present, it must necessarily possess correctness; and when words, conditions, and correctness are present, they must necessarily possess the conditions for speech.
To realize one necessarily entails possessing all three;
the three are themselves the one.
Do not cling to the words and thereby harm the perfection of the teaching, nor falsely misrepresent the intent of the Sage.
If that is so, then nine elements possess the nature of three types of causes:

they are the revealing cause (*vijñapti-hetu*) for defilement, the contributory cause (*pratyaya-hetu*) for evil, and the direct cause (*samyag-hetu*) for both the defiled and the evil. These two—defilement and evil—are not distinct; thus, they constitute the direct cause for evil.
How could it be merely a localized cultivation?
It is the nature of the three causes within the Buddha-realm: the causal nature of goodness as the condition, and the causal nature of purity as the revealing cause.
The non-duality of perfect purity is the excellent primary cause.
This nature is also termed "innate goodness" and "innate evil," or alternatively,
"clarity of principle" and "obscurity of principle."
It is sometimes called the essence of the dual quiescence of permanence and impermanence,
as in the *Avalokiteśvara-sūtra*;
or it is simply named "poisonous harm."
Poisonous harm is identical to the nature of evil;

these are all different names for the same single essence. Their variations in breadth and brevity arise from the differences in the sharpness or dullness of sentient beings' faculties according to their circumstances.
Briefly stated, there are ten realms; extensively stated, there are three thousand.
Thus, one knows that good and evil do not transcend these ten realms.
The natures of these ten realms are fused and mutually inclusive, forming one hundred realms.
The ten suchnesses of the realms constitute one thousand suchnesses.
There are one thousand provisional names,
one thousand five aggregates, and one thousand lands.
Thus, this single thought-moment of deluded, evil cultivation manifesting before us in the three thousand worlds is primordially complete;
it is not produced through artificial effort,
nor does it arise from the generation of marks.
It is not that they contain one another;
a single thought-moment does not exist before,
and the three thousand realms do not exist after.
In a single thought there is nothing lacking, and in the three thousand realms there is nothing in excess.
You must know that while the mind can be broken, the Dharma cannot be broken;
yet even attachment to the Dharma becomes an illness and must likewise be broken.
Thus, good and evil, purity and defilement, are the essential principle and substance of this Dharma-gate;
its substance is fundamentally luminous and pure, without the slightest interruption.
This constitutes severance and realization, delusion and awakening.
This discussion is based solely on the distinction between defilement and purity.
Yet, people of the past lacked the eye of discernment;
they failed to distinguish between principle and circumstance, and could not differentiate between the medicine and the illness.
As soon as one hears in the air that the name "obstructing" means that not even a single characteristic can be established,
one immediately interprets this as a state of annihilation; yet, when the provisional contemplation (假觀) is named,
the illumination of the three thousand [realms] is seen to be perfectly manifest.
Regarding "establishment," this refers to the establishment of the three thousand dharmas.
If all three truths were equally negated,
how could one establish anything?
Delusive passions must be shattered;
therefore, one employs the principle that they are simultaneously empty, provisionally existent, and the Middle Way.
Thus, one penetrates this single thought-moment of the defiled mind of cultivation.
This is precisely the three thousand wondrous realms.
Since cultivated evil is identical to inherent evil,
this is the principle of the three thousand as inherently possessed.
Yet this cultivation of evil is precisely the three thousand wonderful phenomena.
By simply contemplating that both the principle and the phenomena are simultaneously sublated and established as the Dharma-realm,
one naturally encompasses the three thousand phenomenal functions.
The three thousand realms are all the true mark; their characteristics are perfectly manifest.
Phenomena and principle are fundamentally fused, not a mere enumeration of dharmas.
Since they do not belong to that which is negated, how could they not be that which is revealed?
Therefore it is said: "The Buddhas do not sever their inherent evil;
the icchantikas do not sever their inherent goodness.
When this single principle is clarified, all obstructions will naturally dissolve.
Question: What kind of good and evil do icchantikas and Buddhas sever?
Answer: Icchantikas sever all cultivated good and fulfill all cultivated evil;
Buddhas sever all cultivated evil and fulfill all cultivated good.
Question: Since the cultivation of good and the cultivation of evil are both sublime matters, they belong to that which is manifested; why then are they called "that which is to be refuted"?
Answer: The cultivation of good and evil is itself the nature of good and evil.
There is nothing to be discussed regarding the cultivation of good or evil,
for this is the meaning of cessation.
All Buddhas have completely severed and exhausted the cultivation of evil.
The icchantika severs and exhausts the cultivation of goodness;
yet since the cultivated good and evil are identical to the inherent nature of good and evil,
how could the cultivation of good and evil ever be severed?
This is the meaning of non-interruption.
Within this lies the subtle essence of both interruption and non-interruption.
Question: How can the nature of goodness and cultivated goodness of an icchantika, which are not interrupted, arise?
Question: Do the Buddhas, who have severed inherent evil (*prakṛti-pāpa*), still give rise to cultivated evil (*bhāvanā-pāpa*)?
Answer: Because the icchantika does not realize inherent goodness (*prakṛti-kuśala*), they are defiled by [the notion of] goodness;
therefore, cultivated goodness (*bhāvanā-kuśala*) can arise.
They extensively remedy all evils.
Because the Buddhas are able to penetrate evil,
they possess mastery over evil, and thus evil no longer arises.
Extensively employing various evil means to transform and deliver sentient beings—
this wondrous functioning that remains untainted is called the "Dharma-gate of Evil.
Although it lacks any characteristic of defilement or obstruction, [it functions thus].
Yet there exists the aspect of the inherent nature-endowment (*xingju*);
for those at the stage of ordinary beings (*bodidì*), it is merely the principle and the name,
and upon first hearing it, the contemplative practice (*guānxíng*) has not yet been manifested.
Examining the body, one remains deluded;
the six sense faculties appear to function,
yet at the first stage of abiding, one attains partial vision, culminating in the perfection of the fruit of wondrous enlightenment.
Ultimate clarity must be personally realized through principle;
only then will its characteristics become manifest.
This is comparable to the story of Lord Cao, whose hidden features were revealed only when he removed his clothes. One may understand this through analogy.
It is as clear as the mutual relationship between Sun Quan and Liu Bei, which is evident before one's eyes.
It is also like the identity of all waves as moisture and all moisture as waves;
while the characteristics of the waves are easy to recognize, the nature of the moisture is difficult to manifest.
In this manner, the principle of phenomena possesses three functions:
the single principle of phenomena is itself the nature of emptiness (śūnyatā),
while the cause of realization is the nature of the provisional (prajñapti).
The conditional cause (pratyaya-hetu) is neutral.
If the three truths (tri-satya) of the direct cause (hetu-hetu) were not intrinsically possessed (prakṛti-pariniṣpanna), by what means could their meaning be established?
Not only are the three thousand [dharmas] identical to the three truths, but the three truths are likewise identical to the three thousand.
Therefore, it is said that the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) encompasses all phenomena,
while the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) dissolves all phenomena.
The conventional truth establishes all dharmas;
the three thousand realms are themselves the Middle,
taking the Middle as primary.
It is one yet three;
this is called the "wondrous object of contemplation that is inherently present.
Because emptiness, the provisional, and the middle are all attributes within the Middle Way, they are identical.
That is, emptiness and the provisional return to the two cultivations.
The three thousand [realms] being identical with emptiness takes emptiness as primary;
this is called "the cultivation arising from the entirety of nature."
This is the wondrous contemplation within the cause.
Since the provisional, the middle, and all are empty, these three all belong to the contemplation of emptiness;
thus, the provisional and the middle return to their function.
The three thousand realms as the provisional (the objective realm) take the provisional as their primary characteristic;
this is called the great function of liberation at the level of the fruit.
This is because both the empty and the middle are provisional, and all three belong to the sphere of function.
The provisional is identical to emptiness, returning to the realm of contemplation;
these three factors are but one,
each clearly corresponding to two aspects.
Discussing the three objects:
the three contemplations and three functions are neither identical nor separate;
they are neither vertical nor horizontal, and are both negation and illumination.
The two meanings are simultaneously profound, wondrous, deep, and absolute,
like the three dots of the letter *ī*,
each distinct and not intermingled with the others.
The three being inseparable is called Mahāparinirvāṇa;
now, we shall discuss the three contemplations from the perspective of the contemplator.
That which is observed is precisely the three truths.
As for what are called the "three contemplations":
because they are identical with emptiness, they shatter defiled and obstructive attachments.
A single characteristic is not established,
because this reveals that these three thousand worlds share the same nature; thus,
all are immediately able to coexist within a single direction.
Because the divergent streams of thought are unified,
like many beads all converging into a single bead;
it is ultimately pure, neither annihilated nor empty.
Because they are precisely provisional, they mutually contain and mutually encompass one another;
all phenomena clearly manifest these three thousand worlds.
Without losing their own essence, each one is identical to all.
Although they coexist within a single thought-moment, they become increasingly distinct;
it is like the reflection of a single jewel entering many jewels—
an inconceivable state that does not depend on provisional conditions.
Because it is precisely the Middle Way, these three thousand worlds are revealed;
they are neither one nor all,
neither partial nor combined.
It simultaneously negates both extremes,
being free from dualistic characteristics while simultaneously illuminating the two truths; thus,
emptiness and the conventional appear vividly and distinctly.
How could this be the same as "only-middle" (but-mid),
which does not possess the principle that "one being empty, all are empty," wherein all three contemplations are empty,
constituting the universal contemplation of emptiness?
All is provisional; the three contemplations are all provisional—this is the general contemplation of the provisional.
All is the Middle Way; the three contemplations are all the Middle Way—this is the general contemplation of the Middle Way.
Thus, throughout the day one deconstructs all characteristics and yet all dharmas are established;
throughout the day one establishes all dharmas and yet not even a speck of dust remains;
throughout the day one severs all dependencies and yet the two extremes blaze forth.
This is the simultaneous breaking and establishing,
the simultaneous establishing and breaking; it is neither breaking nor establishing, yet through non-breaking and non-establishing, there is breaking and establishing.
It is also called "negation as illumination" and "illumination as negation";
it is neither negation nor illumination, yet it is both negation and illumination.
Although it is said that they proceed sequentially, they exist simultaneously.
If this were so, there would be no logical ground for establishing non-existence, nor would there be any refutation of insentient things.
How could this be consistent with the emptiness of negation and the conventionality dependent upon conditions?
Is this not to speak of departing from the two extremes and abiding in the middle?
Therefore it is said:
"Only a Buddha and a Buddha can exhaustively fathom [this]."
Even the two vehicles of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, as numerous as grains of rice and hemp, and bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges,
are all unable to know even a small fraction of this meaning.
Thus, these three thousand [worlds] universally rely upon the various sections that reside within the Lotus Sūtra.
This is because the former scriptures suffered from two faults: first, the error of overlapping inclusion;
second, the deficiency of partiality and separation.
Now, this sutra is not only pure and unadulterated,
but it can also reveal that the coarse is itself the sublime; thus,
its title is called "The Sublime Dharma" (Saddharmapuṇḍarīka).
It truly lies herein.
Thus we know that those who take this wondrous Dharma of absolute transcendence as the essence of contemplation are like sunlight,
which does not coexist with darkness.
This is the ultimate, final, and most profound teaching;
it is the authentic mind-seal transmitted from Buddha to Buddha.
The Buddha transmitted it to Kāśyapa.
Kāśyapa transmitted it to Ānanda,
and so on until the twenty-fourth generation, when it was passed to the bhikṣu Siṃha.
Siṃha encountered difficulties and was unable to transmit it.
This constitutes the ancestral transmission from the Golden Mouth;
all those who "knew it through seeing" appear in the *Dharma-Transmission Records*.
Some versions add six Buddhas at the beginning and four patriarchs at the end.

The delivery of the Dharma through the recitation of verses and the picking of a flower with a smile were proclaimed as a "separate transmission outside the scriptures"; however, as there are no scriptural or treatise authorities for this,
everyone rejects it.
By the time of Emperor Ming of the Han dynasty, the Buddha-dharma had flowed eastward; during the Northern Qi period,
there was Master Huiwen, who,
through his investigation of the *Śāstra on the Mahāyāna-samparigraha*, awakened to the single mind and the threefold wisdom.
The founder of the Horizontal School (Hengzong) traced it back to Nāgārjuna;
he was the thirteenth master among the twenty-four patriarchs.
Master Wen, for his part, came to know of it through hearing.
He transmitted this to Nanyue,
who successfully realized the Samādhi of the Lotus Sūtra and attained the purity of the six sense faculties.
He, in turn, transmitted it to Tiantai.
At the sacred peak of Tiantai, he personally received the Great Awakening;
his wondrous realization was sustained through stillness,
and his realization was attained not by means of another.
Using the wondrous purport of the Lotus Sūtra,
he formed the "Three Thousandfold World of Non-referential Wondrous Contemplation" and transmitted it to Zhang’an.
Zhang’an compiled the Dharma-treasury and transmitted it to Erwei;
Erwei transmitted it to Zuoxi;
and Zuoxi transmitted it to Jingxi.
Jingxi extensively composed biographies to support and elucidate the Great Meaning,
making it as clear as the sun and stars;
he further propagated these teachings downward.
Those who saw it all and knew it were such that the teachings of this single family illuminated the four seas.
Initially, they faced the upheaval caused by An Lushan; subsequently, they suffered the abolition during the Huichang era.
Later, due to the wars and fires of the Five Dynasties, the collection of teachings was utterly destroyed,
nearly reaching the point of no longer being transmitted.
Luoxi searched for it in vain.
I have long heard that he was as comprehensive in his knowledge as a net casting over the world.
When the King of Qian sent envoys to Goryeo and Japan,
Jiaoguan returned to Wuxing, while Wuxing returned to Jiangzhe.
The transmission reached Siming;
what Jingxi had not recorded, he recorded.
Those three samādhis that are difficult to practice, he practiced them all.
The restoration of this Way is like the great brightness in the sky, which cannot be obscured;
this too is something known through hearing.
Therefore, Liang Jingzhi of the Hanlin Academy said that it refutes the hundred schools and surpasses all other doctrines;
while Liu Zhitou of the Yuanwai Office said that it is increasingly distant from the Sage.
Heterodox views arose concurrently;
only the Great Master of Tiantai attained the true teaching.
How could these two worthies have flattered him with empty praise?
Since the various schools do not know that evil dharmas are inherent in nature,
when they discuss the nine realms, they speak only of "nature-arising" (xingqi).
Even if some were to claim that the Perfect Teaching takes the inherent nature as its central tenet, [they would still be mistaken].
One knows only that nature is endowed with goodness;
one does not know that nature is endowed with evil.
Thus, although it is said that afflictions are identical to bodhi, [the underlying reason remains unapprehended].
Birth-and-death is itself nirvana.
The words of the "mice squeaking and birds chirping" are mere talk without substance;
one must necessarily overturn the nine realms and transform evil practice.
It realizes the goodness of the Buddha-realm nature,
leading to the direct pointing to the human mind to see one's nature and become a Buddha,
as expressed in such teachings as "the mind itself is the Buddha."
This refers to the true mind attaining Buddhahood,
not the deluded mind. Therefore, some have said:
"This very mind is Buddha.
Is it the true mind?
Or is it the deluded mind?
The answer is: it is the true mind.
Furthermore, some say: "Cultivation and realization are not non-existent."
Defilement is thus precluded;
this alone designates the pure Dharmakāya as the school of the separate transmission outside the teachings.
The Selection says: "The Reward and Transformation bodies are not the True Buddha, nor are they the speakers of the Dharma.
Nevertheless, the great function and great efficacy are not without the Reward and Transformation bodies.
If one understands that transformation is communicated through penetration, one is then obstructed by defilement;
because the conditions are not those of protective mindfulness, one cannot suddenly perceive the Dharma-body.
All of these do not transcend the meaning of being "only within."
One is still unable to know the Buddha-realm.
Since it is merely the neutral [nature] that possesses the three bodies, how could it know the three bodies of the nine realms?
When speaking in terms of good and evil, it is biased toward the nature of goodness.
In terms of the ten realms, it belongs specifically to the Buddha-realm;
in terms of the true and the deluded, it belongs specifically to the True;
and in terms of the nine consciousnesses, it belongs specifically to the eternally pure, true consciousness.
In terms of the four teachings, this belongs specifically to the Distinct Teaching (Bie-jiao).
In terms of the ten objects such as the aggregates (skandhas), it pertains to the realm of the Bodhisattva.
One has not yet escaped the three obstacles and the four demons.
What is called the "Sudden and Perfect Mind-Seal"?
Therefore, one should know that when the various masters speak of "pointing directly to the true," they mean pointing directly to the true;
it does not mean pointing to the delusory and calling it the true.
In that case, it should simply be said that "bodhi is bodhi" and "nirvāṇa is nirvāṇa.
Since it is not demonstrated as being identical with the aggregates, [it cannot be so characterized].
Furthermore, there is no characteristic of cultivation or arousal [of the path].
This refers exclusively to the True Mind of the Buddha-realm, wherein one aspect is negated and another is established.
If this were not the Separate Teaching (biejiao), which posits the severance of the nine grades of delusion through the contemplation of principle, with what else could it be compared?
Furthermore, they fail to understand that inherent evil is merely another name for Buddha-nature; thus,
they hold that afflictions, the deluded mind, and the form of birth-and-death are all devoid of Buddha-nature.
Because the defiled mind lacks Buddha-nature,
the Dharma-character school (Lakṣaṇavāda) maintains that those of the two vehicles with fixed natures and the most evil icchantikas will not attain Buddhahood.
Because the form of birth-and-death lacks Buddha-nature,
the proponents of the Nature School (Xingzong) claim that walls, tiles, and rubble cannot attain Buddhahood. One must, however,
destroy the afflictions, birth-and-death, and cultivated evils of the nine realms.
This is because it reveals the nature of the Buddha-realm and the goodness of the Buddha-nature;
yet, while one may know that the state of fruition is all-pervasive,
one does not understand that the causal mind is inherently complete.
If that were so, it would not only mean that insentient things lack intrinsic nature, but sentient beings as well.
For what reason must one speak of "Mind-Only" in reference to True Suchness (tathatā)?
It is because this establishes that Vairocana possesses the Buddha-nature and is eternally real form.
If it is said that only form constitutes the serene light (sukhāvatī) possessing Buddha-nature,
what does this have to do with the afflictions of sentient beings' minds or the insentient matter of birth-and-death?
This is explained in detail in the *Jinbi* (The Golden Scalpel).
Question: Some say that Nanyue and Tiantai instructed one to cultivate the three types of cessation and the three types of contemplation based on the principle of the three truths.
Although these teachings and their meanings are indeed perfect and subtle, [is this not so?]
However, the sequence for entering the gate is likewise nothing other than the four dhyānas and eight samādhis cultivated by eminent monks;
as for the characteristics of these various meditative states, only that transmitted by Bodhidharma is sudden and identical to the Buddha-body.
Now, what is the contradiction in this which has been clarified?
The answer is: it is simply because others see that our school establishes the sixth consciousness as the objective realm of the aggregates (*skandha*) for contemplation.

To claim that what is elucidated by the provisional teachings requires one to contemplate the ninth consciousness before attaining identity with the Buddha-body is an erroneous refutation of the gravest kind.
Although this has already been analyzed above, it shall now be further evaluated.
As for the object of cognition, one should focus solely on what is proximate and essential;
that is, the sixth consciousness-mind.
Taking this as the object of contemplation,
one knows that the wondrous three consciousnesses have never for a moment been separated from a single seeing or a single thinking;
although there is but a single consciousness, it is never not contemplated by means of the three consciousnesses.
It has never been the case that the three consciousnesses do not take [phenomena] as their objects.
If one were to directly use this mind to take the reality-mark (dharmatā) of the Buddha-realm as its object, it would be like attempting to suspend a mountain with a lotus fiber;
it would only increase discursive thought, making it impossible to reach the state of no-thought.
Why is this? Since this sixth consciousness arises from the perfuming of both views and afflictions,
it is capable of giving rise to the discrimination of longing and aversion, thereby acting as the cause for wholesome and unwholesome deeds.
This is precisely the substance of cultivated evil;
this cultivated evil is itself innate evil.
This constitutes the observing dharma that is capable of observation.
Furthermore, this is the dharma-gate that is revealed; thus Jingxi said:
"Suddenly, one has not yet even heard the name of 'inherent evil in nature'."
How could one believe in the existence of practices based on inherent virtue?
This is because the cultivated evil is identical to the inherent evil;
thus, within the three contemplations and ten stages of practice, there are no delusions to be destroyed and no principles to be revealed.
This is what is called the wondrous practice of non-action;
it extends even to the fruit stage, wherein the form-body manifests universally,
assuming forms within the nine realms and sporting within the six paths of existence.
When the entire nature of evil arises, it is called responding without deliberation.
If, however, one were to transform evil into good, severing evil and realizing good,
then practice would be established through effort within the causal stage, and there would be activity upon the resultant stage.
How does mental application and supernatural power differ from those of the non-Buddhists?
To claim that such things are suddenly identical to the Buddha-body is to mistake fish eyes for bright pearls.
To point to a mountain pheasant and call it a phoenix—
though even a child of three feet would know this to be erroneous—
so it is with positing "evil nature" in opposition to "good nature."
Regarding the sequential discussion of the ten realms:
the six realms are considered evil, while the two vehicles are considered good;
the eight realms are considered evil, while the bodhisattvas are considered good.
The nine realms are evil and the Buddha-realm is good;
these nine and the one are precisely the limit of evil and the pinnacle of goodness.
Therefore, what is being discussed here concerns the perfect teaching (*yuanjiao*), which asserts that human nature inherently possesses both good and evil.
Therefore, like a gentleman who is not limited to a single vessel,
one is able to embody both good and evil as non-dual in essence and function;
whereas others do not possess this capacity for inherent evil.
Therefore, just as a truly good person cannot commit evil,
it is only when one is led astray by ignorance that one is able to commit evil.
The *Śāstra* says:
Sensual desire itself is the Way;
so too are delusion and anger.
Within these three dharmas, all the Buddha-dharmas are fully contained.
Lust, ignorance, and anger are the cultivation of evil.
To be endowed with all Buddha-dharmas is precisely the nature of evil.
Furthermore, a sutra says:
By snapping their fingers, scattering flowers, and bowing with palms joined, they all attain the Way of the Buddha.
"Snapping fingers" and so forth refer to the cultivation of goodness;
"all attaining the Way of the Buddha" refers to the inherent goodness of nature.
In this way, there are none among the sentient beings of the dharma realm who do not return to this very original self-nature; thus,
even those scholars dwelling in mountain forests and marshy wetlands attain it.
He thoroughly investigated the Buddha Vehicle and widely proclaimed the holy transformation.
Some he came to know through direct instruction and personal guidance from his teachers;
others he came to know by studying the subtle points and unraveling hidden meanings within the commentaries on the sutras.
When seeing and hearing, two minds illuminate one another;
when the profound is grasped through silent resonance, it is called "transmission.
Since my own mind is inherently complete and does not depend on others, it is called "non-transmission."
Although the mind is inherently possessed [of this nature], it is only through pointed instruction that one comes to know it;
thus, this is called "transmission. This wondrous state of non-transmission is like a seal: the mind itself is the seal, hence it is named the "Mind-Seal" (Cittamudrā).
One who knows this is said to possess "wondrous understanding."
One who practices this is said to possess "sublime conduct";
one who realizes this is said to possess "sublime fruit.
In this way, one's task is fully accomplished.
As discussed above, this pertains only to one's own practice and does not yet involve the transformation of others.
For instance, Kāśyapa attained awakening upon hearing a single metaphorical teaching, without requiring further cultivation.
Because he fully received and practiced the teachings bestowed during the five periods,
it is said that his preaching of the Dharma was based upon this; thus, his practice of giving was opened to complete mastery,
and he subsequently received the Tathāgata’s confirmation and bestowal of a prophecy.
Thus we know that Kāśyapa transmitted this mind-seal through the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
"Hearing the parable" refers to wondrous understanding;
"awakening and entering" refers to the wondrous fruit.
Therefore it is said:
"Now the great treasure of the Dharma King has arrived spontaneously.
Since it is so for Kāśyapa, it may be understood by analogy for others as well.
Since the Golden Mouth [of the Buddha] was thus, the Master is likewise so now.
Bei Qi attained a brilliant and sudden awakening upon first reading the text;
Nan Yue realized it after ninety days.
It was only after twenty-eight days that Tiantai attained realization;
thus we know that one proceeds from hearing to reflection,
and through reflection and cultivation, one attains realization.
Because the capacities of their faculties differ, there is variation in the speed of their realization.
When discussing the transformation of others, this is termed "entrustment" (付託) and is also called "bequeathing" (囑累).
There are still both general and specific [applications].
The general applies to all four assemblies;
the specific pertains to Kāśyapa.
Just as he exhorted them to uphold, recite, and entrust [the teachings] for their circulation,
and even instructed, benefited, and gladdened them regarding other profound dharmas,
there were eight thousand śrāvakas present.
The bodhisattvas are immeasurable and innumerable;
specifically, it is only Kāśyapa who [receives] them,
yet the entrustment is not restricted to a single location.
Therefore, although he was not present in the assembly during the Nirvana, he wished to ensure that the fourfold assembly would all know and revere his presence;
thus he said: "The unsurpassed True Dharma that I now possess..."
He entrusted [the teaching] to Mahākāśyapa.
Furthermore, the *Dharmapada-śāstra* (Fu fachuán) states:
"As his work of transformation was nearing completion and he was about to enter parinirvāṇa..."
He addressed his great disciple Mahākāśyapa:
"As I am now about to enter parinirvāṇa,
I entrust this profound Dharma to you."
"You should, in the future, respectfully follow my intention and propagate this widely so that it is not allowed to be interrupted. If such were the case,
there would certainly be texts [of the sutra] that have not been fully translated."
There are three reasons why [the Dharma] was entrusted solely to Kāśyapa:
first, while the conditions for the Tathāgata were fading away, the conditions for Kāśyapa were flourishing;
second, Kāśyapa’s ascetic practices could cause the Buddha-dharma to abide for a long time.
Third, it is easy to practice the guidance and transformation [of others] by relying on minor fruits;

for example, this is like the Buddha Pure Bright Virtue (Vimalaprabhāsa) entrusting [the Dharma] to the Bodhisattva Joyful Vision of All Beings (Sarvasattvapriyadarśana) so that it may be widely disseminated.
This is because the conditions for it did not lie there.
Therefore, it was entrusted to this [Kāśyapa]; how could it be that the Buddha’s mind-seal was transmitted only to Kāśyapa while all others remained ignorant?
The people of this world are deluded by this and deceive the sages and worthies, giving rise to groundless sophistry.
They have not yet been able to understand the purport of this transmission regarding self-cultivation and the transformation of others. Alas!
This constitutes a peerless masterpiece of all time within a single school, the authentic transmission of the Buddhas and Patriarchs;
yet, like "White Snow" or "Yangchun," its lofty melody finds few who can harmonize with it.
Nevertheless, having fortunately encountered this auspicious era, I do not decline to set down these humble and unrefined words.
I have repeatedly relied upon paper and ink to broaden my见闻 (knowledge and experience),
emulating the Lotus Sūtra’s fields and villages,
and the Nirvāṇa Sūtra’s trees and stones.
Some may even give rise to slander and disparagement;
I hope only that we may be as fierce and poisonous as beasts crossing a river—
how could we dare concern ourselves with wetting our tails?
The Record of the Transmission of the Buddha’s Mind-Seal at Tiantai concludes.
